front: Why does a trade-execution system care about P99.9 latency, not P50?
back: P99.9 represents the tail latency where one in 1000 orders suffers excessive delay. In trading, even rare, multi-microsecond delays are unacceptable for SLA compliance. P50 is meaningless if P99.9 is 100x worse.

front: You benchmark on your MacBook and EC2, getting different numbers. Which do you quote on your resume and why?
back: EC2 isolated core with turbo off. It's reproducible and fair, unlike a shared MacBook. The MacBook numbers are useful for 'is this broken?' but reflect your specific hardware, not the system's true performance.

front: Your system does 1M orders/sec at P50=1 us. What is the raw latency budget (in CPU cycles) for a single order on a 3 GHz CPU?
back: 1M orders/sec = 1 order per microsecond = 1 order per 3000 CPU cycles (at 3 GHz). Entire order must execute in ~3000 cycles. Typical breakdown: 10-20% memory, 30% tree ops, 50% matching.

front: Describe the data structure for a single price level in an order book. Why that structure?
back: A deque (queue) of orders at that price level. FIFO respects price-time priority: best price first, then earliest arrival first. O(1) pop from front for matching, O(1) push to back for new orders.

front: A sell order arrives and there are 5 buy orders at or above the sell price. Walk through the matching loop.
back: Scan buy orders from best price down until you hit a price below the sell price. For each buy, compute fill = min(remaining buy, remaining sell). Allocate a fill record, emit it. If sell exhausted, break; if buy exhausted, move to next.
